claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent shift between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
At low temperature and high strain rate, limited thermal activation suppresses dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Suppressed dislocation mobility at low temperature and high strain rate promotes deformation twinning.
Deformation twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The increased twin density raises strain hardening.
Twinning under low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading preserves the alloy's strength-ductility balance.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will produce a significant increase in twin density relative to room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate loading.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will increase yield strength and strain-hardening rate.
At high temperature and low strain rate, enhanced dislocation mobility favors slip over twinning.
Predominant dislocation slip at high temperature and low strain rate lowers strain hardening.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate loading will produce lower yield strength and greater ductility.
At room temperature and moderate strain rate, FeNiCrMn exhibits a mixture of dislocation slip and limited twinning.
The room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate mechanism mixture yields balanced strength and ductility.
The proposed as-cast FeNiCrMn initial state has a uniform, fine-grained microstructure.
Post-solidification processing or substantial grain coarsening may change the proposed deformation-mechanism relationship.
The hypothesis may cease to apply where crack initiation or void growth dominates deformation.
